# Working With a Coding Agent {#sec-assistant}



Since 2024 the developer Simon Willison has put one request to most new AI models:
"Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle." An SVG is a drawing written as text, so a
model writes one the way it writes code. Below are twelve answers,
from four models. Every one is recognisably a pelican on a bicycle, and they did not cost
the same. Before you look at the prices, guess: how many times dearer was the dearest
than the cheapest that was good enough?

Each row is one model and each column an *effort* level, how long the model reasons before
answering. The dearest cost 13\.09 cents, about 93
times as much as the cheapest that was good enough, at 0\.14 cents.

Choosing between those drawings is the first of many judgements this chapter teaches. A
*coding agent* is a program that writes and edits files and runs commands at your
request: you write the *Prompt*, it does the typing, and you *Check* whether the result is
right. It can produce in a minute what would take an hour by hand, and it can produce
plausible, confident, wrong work just as quickly. How do you get the first kind of work
without being fooled by the second?

::: opener
- Explain how a model and a harness divide the work, and which half to change when an
  agent disappoints.
- Choose a model and effort level for a task, and keep a session's cost down with `/model`,
  `/clear` and `/exit`.
- Decide where to start an agent, which of its commands to approve and which rules belong
  in `AGENTS.md`.
- Write a prompt that names its files, asks for one step and ends in a check, and size a
  larger task by how it can be checked.
:::

If you already use an agent every day, read @sec-three-skills to @sec-boxes and skim the rest.

## Model plus harness {#sec-model-harness}

A coding agent is two programs working together (@fig-agent-loop).

The **model** is a large language model, such as Anthropic's Claude, OpenAI's GPT or
Google's Gemini. It runs on the vendor's servers. It reads text and writes text, and it can
reply with a structured request to use a tool: "read this file", "run this command".

The **harness** is the program on your computer that surrounds the model. Claude Code,
Codex, Antigravity and OpenCode are harnesses. The harness gives the model its tools (reading and
writing files, running commands, searching), carries out the model's tool requests, asks you
before it does anything consequential, and sends the results back to the model. That loop
repeats until the model replies with an answer instead of another request, and it is what
makes the pair an *agent*: it acts in your project folder, one tool request after another,
until the step is done, where a web chat hands you text to copy.

A short way to remember the split: **the model decides, the harness does, you direct and
check.** It has a practical consequence. Many harnesses can run several models, so the same
harness behaves differently with a different model, and the same model behaves differently
inside a different harness. When an agent disappoints you, the cause can be either half,
and the fix is different: a stronger model for reasoning that falls short, better rules or
permissions for a harness that does the wrong thing.

![How a coding agent works: the harness carries out the model's requests in your project folder, and asks you before it runs a command (OpenCode, by default, does not).](../media/diagrams/agent-loop){#fig-agent-loop .on-light fig-alt="You give the harness a prompt, and it shows you results and asks you to approve commands. The harness (Claude Code, Codex or Antigravity) sends the conversation and tool results to the model (Claude, GPT or Gemini), which runs on the vendor's servers and replies with text or a request to use a tool. The harness carries out tool requests in the project folder, its root: it reads AGENTS.md first, then reads and edits files and runs commands there. The model decides, the harness does, and you direct and check."}

::: why
The model cannot touch your computer. Everything it "does" is a request that the harness
carries out, and the harness can show you each request before acting on it. That is the
basis of every safety habit in this chapter: you approve commands you have read, and you
review files after they change.
:::

## Choosing an agent and a model {#sec-choose}

This book covers four agents. The first three come from the same company as their default
models; OpenCode, an open-source harness, runs whichever model you connect to it:

| Agent | You type | Default models |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Code, by Anthropic | `claude` | Claude |
| Codex, by OpenAI | `codex` | GPT |
| Antigravity, by Google | `agy` | Gemini |
| OpenCode, an open-source project | `opencode` | any you connect |

: The agents this book covers. {#tbl-assistants}

Every prompt in the book is written to work in all four, and the install command, account
and rules file of each were checked against its documentation. A vendor's own pairing of
harness and model is the easiest to set up, but it is not automatically the best fit for a
task: the harness and the model are separate choices.

### Pick a model by task, not by rank

Each vendor offers a family of models, from small and cheap to large and capable. They are
not simply better and worse versions of one thing. Larger, more recent models usually follow
longer instructions, plan multi-step work and recover from their own errors better. Small
models are faster and cheaper, and often good enough for short, well-specified edits such as
fixing a typo or reformatting a table. Joining two datasets or debugging a failed render
rewards the stronger model.

The prompts in this book are short and specific, so a mid-sized model at a moderate effort
setting is enough: Claude's Sonnet on medium effort\, or Haiku for small edits\, or OpenAI's Sol on low. For unfamiliar, hard work, the
vendors' own advice starts higher: Anthropic suggests starting with Opus 5\.5 for most workloads\, and OpenAI with GPT\-6 Astra for complex reasoning and coding. The names
change every few months, and @sec-facts keeps the current ones; the advice does not. Start small, and move
up only when a task keeps failing.

Some routes to a model cost nothing at all; @sec-before-setup gives them, and what to check
before you use one.

Models are priced by the *token*, a fragment of text of a few characters, with one rate for
the text sent to the model (input) and another for the text it writes (output). List prices
are *API* prices: what a program pays per token when it sends requests to the model
directly, through the vendor's programming interface (the API), rather than through a
monthly subscription.

::: practice
**Prices change monthly; the principle does not.** When last checked, the list prices of the
eight models in @tbl-prices ran from \$0\.50 to
\$50 per million output tokens, a 100-fold
spread between the smallest and the largest. That table, with its sources, is in @sec-facts,
the one place this book keeps facts that change; read it as a snapshot of the spread, not as
numbers to plan with. Subscriptions count usage differently, and which models you can choose
depends on your plan and the agent's version.
:::

The price of a fixed level of capability has been falling fast, though perhaps not at the
frontier (the studies are in Further reading), so choose by what the task needs, not by
today's price.

Checked 2026\-11\-12;
@sec-facts has each source.

### One prompt, four models, three efforts

The pelicans this chapter opened with make the trade-off concrete: one run of each of four
Claude models at three effort levels, each reply priced at API list prices (@fig-pelicans).
The Fable row is Fable 5.1, Fable 5.2's predecessor, at its list price of 10 / 50 dollars per
million tokens. Read the grid in two directions. Down the rows, the model grows and the price
per token rises, so costs climb from fractions of a cent to more than ten cents. Across the columns, effort
rises: the model reasons longer and writes more, so the cost usually rises while the picture
gains details rather than becoming correct. Haiku on low effort has the weakest frame; from
medium effort up, the frames are sound, which is consistent with, though no proof of, the
book's advice of medium effort.

Keep the evidence in proportion. It is one run per cell of one small, self-contained task,
not a benchmark: run it again and you get different birds, and Fable on medium effort even
cost less than Fable on low. More effort is not always better, either: at maximum effort,
Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 each spent their whole output limit of 128,000 tokens reasoning, and
returned no drawing. A drawing says little about a long job that joins datasets and recovers
from errors, which is where stronger models earn their price. Whether a 93-fold difference in
price is worth paying depends entirely on the task.

## What a conversation costs {#sec-cost}

Whether you pay by subscription or by API, use is counted in tokens. Three things raise the
cost of a session:

1. **A bigger model** costs more per token.
2. **A higher effort setting** makes the model write more reasoning tokens per reply.
3. **A longer conversation** costs more with every turn, because the model keeps no memory
   between requests: the harness sends the whole conversation again each time. Everything
   sent with a request (the conversation so far, the files read, the project's rules) is the
   model's *context*. Prompt caching makes the repeated part cheaper, not free, and caches
   expire.

The habits that follow are simple: a mid-sized model at moderate effort, one task per
conversation, and a fresh conversation as soon as a task is done. Three commands, typed into
the agent itself rather than run in the terminal (@sec-two-places), cover them:

| Command | Use it when |
|---|---|
| `/model` | another model or effort level: when a prompt keeps failing (go up) or the work is routine (go down) |
| `/clear` | a new conversation with empty context, when one task ends and an unrelated one starts |
| `/exit` | leaves the agent, when you are done or need another folder |

: Three commands that control cost and context; wording differs by agent, so type `/` to list yours. {#tbl-slash}

OpenCode's names differ, and @sec-cheatsheet lists them.

`/clear` matters for quality as well as cost. Old instructions and files read earlier keep
steering the model while they remain in the conversation; a fresh conversation drops them.
Nothing on disk changes, and the project's rules file is read again.

::: think
One task is finished and an unrelated one starts. Which command first, and what does it keep?

`/clear`. The new task needs none of the old conversation, and carrying it along costs
tokens on every turn and can mislead the model. Your files stay as they are, and the
project's rules file is read again.
:::

## The root folder is the agent's world {#sec-root-folder}

<!-- The two trust prompts as Claude Code 2.1.319 and Codex 0.167.0 printed them, captured
2026-11-07 (03-setup.qmd, Step 3). -->

An agent treats the folder you start it in as its *root*: it reads and edits files there
and in the folders below, and runs commands from there. The first time you start one in a
new folder, it asks whether you trust it. Claude Code's prompt warns that "Claude Code'll be
able to read, edit, and execute files here"; Codex asks the same question in a folder that is
a Git repository, and says it can read, edit and run files "subject to your permission
settings".

That question deserves a real answer. Trust only a folder you created for the work. Never
start an agent in your home folder, in Documents, or anywhere that holds other people's
projects, private documents or keys (such as `~/.ssh`). Project instructions in a trusted
folder are read and followed too, which is another reason to trust only your own folders.

OpenCode, by default, asks neither question: not whether to trust the folder, and not before
it acts. @sec-step-assistant shows how to make it ask.

Starting in a small project folder has three practical benefits. Paths in prompts stay short
(`data/attractions.csv`), the project's rules file is found, and a mistake stays inside one
folder that you can restore. It is not a guaranteed boundary, though: a command can still
name a path outside the folder, so read each command before you approve it.

::: pitfall
Two agents writing the same files, or rendering in one folder at once, will collide;
@sec-sub-agents shows the safe split. To work on another project, leave with `/exit`, change
folder, and start the agent again there.
:::

## Rules that persist: `AGENTS.md` {#sec-agents-md}

Everything you tell an agent in conversation is forgotten when the conversation ends.
Rules that must hold in every session go in a file: `AGENTS.md`, a plain Markdown file at the
top of the project folder that the agent reads at the start of each session. A good one
has three parts:

- **Scope:** what the project is, and what it is not.
- **Rules:** what must always hold ("every number comes from a cited file in `data/`").
- **Commands:** how to build and check the project.

All four agents read it. Claude Code reads it when there is no `CLAUDE.md`, or through a
one-line `CLAUDE.md` that imports it (`@AGENTS.md`), as the repository behind this book does;
@sec-facts has where each agent looks.

::: pitfall
`AGENTS.md` is context, not enforcement. The agent reads the rules and usually follows
them, but it can still slip. Write rules that are concrete enough to check ("call ALVA counts
'ALVA member attractions'"), and check them.
:::

::: think
Yesterday you told the agent, in conversation, to say "ALVA member attractions". Today it
writes "top attractions". Why, and what is the lasting fix?

The instruction ended with yesterday's conversation: the model keeps no memory between
sessions. Put the rule in `AGENTS.md`, which is read at the start of every session, and still
check for it, because rules are context, not enforcement.
:::

Part II writes the London guide's rules in @sec-markdown, and the water analysis writes its
analysis's in @sec-water-question.

## How to ask for work {#sec-prompting}

A *prompt* is the request you type into the agent. Four habits make prompts reliable:

**Be specific.** Name the files, the columns, the chart type and the output. "Make a chart"
invites guessing; "add a horizontal bar chart of `visits_2025` by `attraction` from
`data/attractions.csv`" does not.

**One step at a time.** One task per prompt keeps each change small enough to review, and
tells you which step broke when one does.

**Ask it to run and check.** End with a check the agent can perform: "render it and tell
me which file it wrote", "check that the PDF is one page". An agent that verifies its own
work catches many of its own mistakes.

**Check what changed.** You are responsible for the result. Read the changed files (most
agents can show you a *diff*, the lines added and removed) before moving on.

When a prompt mentions something you do not understand (a YAML key, a Markdown construct, a
Python call), ask before you paste:

::: {.prompt}
```default
Explain what a Markdown table is and when to use it. Then name the official docs page where I can verify your answer.
```
:::

Asking for the documentation page matters: it turns the answer into something you can check.

### A web chat can draft your prompt

If you know what you want but not how to ask for it, a free web chat (Claude, ChatGPT or
Gemini in the browser) can turn a rough idea into a prompt. Describe the goal in plain words,
name your tools, and ask for a prompt of one to four lines, with one task, concrete file names
and a check (@fig-chat-prompt). The chat cannot see your files, so it guesses; the agent
can see them, so it checks. Read the drafted prompt before you paste it, and fix any file name
that does not match your folder.

![A web chat drafts a prompt, you read it, and the coding agent runs it. An illustration drawn for the workshop, not a recording: real replies vary.](../media/gifs/chat-prompt.gif){#fig-chat-prompt .anim fig-alt="An animated example in five steps. A free web chat gets a request typed in plain words: a one-page London visitor guide, and a prompt for a coding agent, naming the tools Quarto and Markdown, of one to four lines with one task, concrete file names and a check. The chat replies with a prompt: use Quarto and Markdown, create london.md with the title Visit London, a level-1 heading and a two-sentence welcome, add a heading Top sights with three bullets each naming a place and why to visit, run quarto render london.md, then list the headings in london.html and any errors. The prompt is copied and pasted into a coding agent in the terminal, which writes london.md, renders it, lists the headings and reports no errors."}

::: pitfall
Paste only what you would be happy to publish. Web chats and agents send your text to
the vendor: no passwords, keys, unpublished data or personal information.
:::

## Vocabulary, specification, verification {#sec-three-skills}

With an agent doing the typing, you need three skills, and every chapter from here on teaches
a format through them rather than through its syntax:

1. **Vocabulary**: knowing what is possible and what it is called, so you can ask for it.
   "Speaker notes", "a cross-reference", "a reference document for Word", "a parameter":
   an agent can produce any of them, but only if you know to ask, and a name gets you the
   real feature where a description gets an improvisation.
2. **Specification**: writing a request the agent can carry out and you can check. It names
   the files, the settings and the result, and it ends with a check. Rules that must hold in
   every session, such as "every number comes from `outputs/`", go in `AGENTS.md`
   (@sec-agents-md), so you state them once.
3. **Verification**: knowing what good output looks like, and confirming it three ways. Read
   the diff, to see what changed; inspect the render, as its reader would; and run the checks
   that can run without you, such as tests and *guards*, lines that stop the render when a
   sentence no longer matches the data (@sec-water-website).

::: think
An agent tells you it "added a citation style". Which of the three skills tells you whether
it did what you needed?

Verification: open the rendered reference list and compare one entry with the style's own
example, and read the diff to see which setting changed. Vocabulary helped you ask for a
*citation style* by name; only verification shows that it is the right one.
:::

## A step or a task? {#sec-step-or-task}

This book's prompts mostly ask for one small step, because a small change is quick to check.
Experienced readers will soon want to hand an agent a larger task: "add a model card", not
five prompts that build one. Size the work by how it will be checked, not by how much typing
it saves.

| Hand over a larger task when | Keep to single steps when |
|---|---|
| you can state the finished result and how to check it | you will only know it is right when you see it |
| the checks run without you: tests, guards, a render | each step needs your judgement before the next |
| the work is on a branch, so undoing it is one command | the change touches data, publishing or other people's work |
| a failure would be loud: a red test, a stopped render | a failure would be quiet: a plausible wrong sentence |

: When to give an agent a larger task. {#tbl-step-or-task}

A larger task needs a larger check. Ask for a short plan first and read it before the agent
starts; have it work on a branch; require it to run the tests and render every output; and
ask it to end by listing what it changed and anything it could not verify. Then review the
whole change as you would a colleague's pull request, file by file, before it reaches the
main line. The professional chapters show this at work: one prompt adds a whole report to an
existing repository, and its checks are a test suite, a guard and a fresh-clone rebuild.

::: practice
When a larger task goes wrong, do not fix it with a longer conversation. Undo it
(`git restore`, or delete the branch), split it into the steps whose checks failed, and ask
for those one at a time.
:::

## How to read the agent boxes {#sec-boxes}

Every hands-on step in this book uses the same three-part box. Here is a simpler version of
the first one you will meet in Part II:

::: {.prompt}
```default
Create london.md with a level-1 heading "Visit London" and one welcome paragraph.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
writes `london.md` · may run `quarto render london.md`
:::

::: {.you}
approve its commands · open `london.html` in your browser
:::

**Ask your coding agent** holds the exact prompt to paste into the agent (in the HTML
edition, with a copy button). **Expect it to run** lists what the agent will probably do,
so you recognise it when it asks for approval; you do not type these yourself. **You do** lists
the few things only you can do: start the agent, sign in to accounts, approve commands, run
a live preview, open results. The agent occupies the terminal tab it runs in, so commands
in a **You do** box go in a second terminal tab opened in the same folder (@sec-two-places).

Together the boxes are one turn of the loop in the book's title. **Ask your coding
agent** is the *Prompt*. **Expect it to run** and **You do** are where you *Check*,
recognising each command before you approve it and opening the result yourself. The render
is the *Publish*. Each exercise closes the loop with **You're done when**: the check, stated
so that you can see whether it passed.

::: pitfall
Approving a command without reading it. Most commands in this book run a tool the prompt named
(`quarto`, `uv`, `git`, `gh`) on files in the project folder. Stop and ask the agent what a
command does before you approve one that deletes files (`rm`), runs as the administrator
(`sudo`), or touches a folder outside the project that the prompt did not name.
:::

## Using AI in research: say it, own it {#sec-ai-policy}

If your work is research, using an agent raises obligations beyond getting the code
right. Journals and funders differ in detail, so read your venue's own policy, but the
International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE), whose recommendations many
journals follow, states a common core:

- **An AI tool is never an author.** Chatbots and other AI-assisted tools "should not be listed
  as authors because they cannot be responsible for the accuracy, integrity, and originality
  of the work".
- **You are responsible for what it produced.** Humans are responsible for any submitted
  material that used AI-assisted technologies, and should review and edit AI output, which
  "can be incorrect, incomplete, or biased". That includes references: AI-generated material
  is not an acceptable primary source.
- **Disclose the use.** Authors describe their use of AI-assisted technologies at submission,
  in the cover letter and in the appropriate section of the work.

Two further rules follow from ordinary research ethics rather than from any one policy. Keep
unpublished manuscripts, participant data and other confidential material out of public AI
tools. And never let a tool generate or alter primary data or images: presenting generated
data as observed is fabrication.

A useful disclosure names the tool and version, the tasks it performed and the checks you
made. The statement for this book, on its copyright page, is written that way. Where it goes
depends on the use: code and analysis belong in the Methods, with enough detail to reproduce
them, which in a Quarto project means the code itself and the project's `AGENTS.md`.

::: think
Which needs a statement: fixing a typo, or computing a table?

Computing a table is analysis: describe it in the Methods, in enough detail to reproduce.
Venues differ on whether language editing needs a statement; ICMJE's recommendations make no
exception for it, so when in doubt, disclose.
:::

## Summary {.unnumbered}

::: keyideas
- The model decides, the harness does, and you direct and check; when an agent
  disappoints, either half can be the cause.
- Choose a model by the task, not by rank: a cheaper model at medium effort is often enough
  for a small step, and since the whole conversation is sent again each turn, start a fresh
  one for each unrelated task.
- Start an agent only in a folder you created for the work, and read each command before
  you approve it.
- Rules that must last go in `AGENTS.md`, which is context, not enforcement, so write them
  concretely enough to check.
- Good prompts are specific, ask for one step and end in a check; in research the agent is
  never an author, and its use is disclosed.
- Learn each format as vocabulary, specification and verification, and hand over a larger
  task only when its checks can run without you.
:::

All of this assumes a computer on which an agent, Quarto and Python work together. If a
terminal and Git are routine, @sec-fast-path is next. If not, @sec-setup gets your computer
ready in six checked steps.
